@carlosparadis ## R/jira.R **parse_jira(jira_issue_comments_path)** - parses a folder of JIRA issue JSON files and returns a named list with two elements, issues and comments, where each element is a data.table containing the relevant issue or comment fields standardized for further processing. **parse_jira_replies_with_comment(data)** (To be replaced with parse_jira_replies()) - Recommended to delete the defined function "parse_jira_replies_with_comment(data)" and replace where it's called with "parse_jira_replies()" ## R/github.R **parse_github_replies(github_issue_path)** - parses GitHub issues, pull requests, comments, and commits from JSON files, and puts them all into one table with columns like who wrote it, the message, and the subject so it’s ready to use. ## R/mail.R **parse_mbox(perceval_path, mbox_path)** - parses an mbox email archive using Perceval, extracts key fields like message ID, sender, recipients, subject, and body, and returns a standardized data.table with consistently renamed columns for further processing. ## R/sentiment_clean.R **clean_jira_data(data)** - Removes bot-generated messages and 'Hudson' from the JIRA dataset. **clean_mbox_data(data, if_clean_vote=FALSE)** (Rename: filter_irrelevant_mbox_messages()) - Removes automated or irrelevant entries from mbox email data such as system-generated messages, Jira or GitHub notifications, and optional vote-related messages. **clean_mbox_comment(data)** (Rename: remove_invalid_or_duplicate_mbox_comments()) - Removes duplicate rows and any comment whose reply_subject doesn’t match a real reply_id in the dataset. **process_mbox_data(data)** (Rename: clean_and_prepare_mbox_subjects()) - Cleans and standardizes mbox email reply subjects, handling encoding issues and removing common prefixes like "Re:". **create_if_comment_column(data)** (Rename: mark_and_uniquify_comments()) - Adds an if_comment column. It marks a row as a comment when its reply_id is different from its reply_subject, and gives each such comment a unique ID so they can be distinguished from each other ## Misc Note: I've given possible function renames but can still be subjected to change. I am going to repurpose this issue to focus on that instead so it is clear cut from #346. # The Notebook of interest The notebook of interest you want to refactor to Kaiaulu is the Sentiment Analysis Rmd: https://github.com/sailuh/haotian_full_kaiaulu_changes/pull/2/files#diff-980991213c4ecb280b6ed0df9b65ed7e85e44e2fbcfc80927b1f45308eaf9781 This notebook takes as input data from the Python Sentiment Notebook. For now, let us presume that the Python Notebook output a .csv, and this Notebook can take it as input (no code calls). There are 3 functions that are very important in this Notebook: * [transform_reply_to_threepartite_network](https://github.com/sailuh/haotian_full_kaiaulu_changes/pull/2/files#r2412173886) * [merge_comments_and_subjects](https://github.com/sailuh/haotian_full_kaiaulu_changes/pull/2/files#r2412175327) * [projection_reply](https://github.com/sailuh/haotian_full_kaiaulu_changes/pull/2/files#r2412177204) What these functions do is take the data from mailing lists, github, and jira and transform into 3 types of networks: The transform_reply_to_threepartite_network() is creating the network at the bottom. Then, merge_comments_and_subjects creates the second (middle one), and finally projection_reply creates the last one. These functions need some cleanup on their names and what they do to fit Kaiaulu architecture. Kaiaulu distinguishes network from graphs in its architecture. A network is a graph with data in it. This means we have functions to create the populated graphs from data (the transform_* functions found on Mail, GitHub, Git, etc), and we have functions that disregard the data and are in charge of computing graph metrics or modifications to it (See Graph module [here](http://itm0.shidler.hawaii.edu/kaiaulu/reference/index.html#-graph-)). The purpose of the distinction is to reduce redundancy. There is no point in creating a "projection" function for every type of data (mail, jira, git, etc), when the graph of all 3 are the same. I would consider this issue a more complex one, hence saving for last. However, it would serve as a stronger purpose and vision to the tasks you did prior to it as a self contained project.

# Abstractions for Capabilities and Data

Hi, I think your proposal is going in the opposite direction of what we want. We should remove any and all dependency to the .csv files, including its format. But before I go too far on this, let me respond to a prior comment:

https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/issues/346#issuecomment-3387514587

This is your proposal of function renaming. I think we should start here. Let's take for example:

> clean_mbox_data(data, if_clean_vote=FALSE) (Rename: filter_irrelevant_mbox_messages())
>
>   Removes automated or irrelevant entries from mbox email data such as system-generated messages,
>    Jira or GitHub notifications, and optional vote-related messages.

Notice what you tell me is the purpose: To remove a) system-generated messages, b.1) JIRA notifications, b.2) GitHub notifications, c) Vote-related messages. Your proposal is that we call all of this "irrelevant". But the moment a user looks at the function **name** your definition of what constitutes irrelevant, and theirs will differ. So the user must go to the description of the function to figure it out. This is not good. Further, notice the single responsibility principle is violated here: There are many things being done, all by one function. What if I want vote-related messages removed, but not notifications? 

This means this function should be refactored (look up refactor method by Martin Fowler). We want a `filter_reply_system_messages()`, a `filter_reply_notifications()`, etc. So long we break each filter criteria in a function, user can assemble their own filter pipeline. 

The next thing you should consider is what `data` is, or more broadly what is the expected input. This is also an important abstraction. If every function in Kaiaulu expects some random table, then the user is bound to depend on the notebooks they are used to make sense, and keep changing the table left and right. Again, this is about abstractions. A variable named `data` is not good, since, well, anything in Kaiaulu is basically data. Notice how I named every function as `reply`. This is because Kaiaulu has functions to parse_replies out of JIRA, GitHub, etc: 

https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/blob/ac522b6fd675230da905c0b54b241904e6c76705/R/jira.R#L699

https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/blob/ac522b6fd675230da905c0b54b241904e6c76705/R/github.R#L20

So, the data table that should be expected is the reply data.table, which is enforced by the parser functions. As they should, since a user will expect a raw data download, and something to parse it. The reply table is an abstraction to data that are comments. GitHub comments, JIRA comments, E-mail comments, maybe in the future discord comments, etc. If platform specific information is needed, then a parse_jira (not a parse_jira_replies) should be used instead. So long this is respected, then all your filter functions can depend on parse_*_replies() functions, which guarantee a consistent reply table. Your filter functions will thus not need to be edited in the future to accommodate a new data source. It is the same principle as the get() functions for the configs in Kaiaulu. 

So your first next step is:

- [ ] Make a new comment proposal (post as a new comment) in the same format as https://github.com/sailuh/kaiaulu/issues/346#issuecomment-3387514587 with the corrections recommended above.

Afterall, once you migrate the capability to Kaiaulu, the Notebook should still run, but now no longer dependent on the .csv. So the filters will depend on the reply table. The filter output should still be a reply table that looks identical, except with fewer rows if the filter criteria is met. Done in this manner, whether the user use any combination of your filters, or none, the pipeline can proceed.

You further should ensure the refresh_() function on each will furnish you the data that is needed in parse_*_replies(), in case when this was being built the abstractions got deteriorated and do not follow what we are discussing here.

# The Exec 

Your exec goal is to furnish the data needed by the Python Notebook, so the sentiment scores are applied to them. Presuming the model is already trained, you need to modify the Python Notebook data loading. Here comes yet another architectural decision. 

Let's consider this first: Can a user in the future decide to run the sentiment notebook with any combination of GitHub, Mail, and JIRA for a project? Yes, because it is the case not every project will use all 3. Indeed, it would be strange a project to use both GitHub and JIRA at the same time. So even though the current code expects a table of 3, from a integration standpoint, our use case needs to accommodate that. 

If that is the case, you would like an exec that can accommodate the filter and export of these different platforms separately. I will leave you to think this through as an exercise and also propose how this would look like, building on the design decisions above.

# From .csv dependencies to /exec calls on the Notebook side

- [ ] When you are clear on the above part of the pipeline, you need to think first on all the .csv file dependencies. Your goal is to replace them with subprocess.run() on the Python notebook, calling the execs to supply the data that are hardcoded to .csvs.

- [ ] Further, you should check if the Python notebook needs an additional function or two to massage the reply table output from the exec into what the rest of the Notebook expects. In the interest of time, I recommend you just create a new function that rename the columns accordingly to match what the rest of the notebook expects. Say, if the Python notebook expects 3 columns, and the R side is outputting 6, then have a new python function in the api/ folder that "Maps" one to another. As every exec/ call will yield the same table format, a single mapper should suffice. Ideally you would correct the rest of the Python Notebook to comply to Kaiaulu format, but a mapper for now suffice just to make sure everything works. 

# The ping pong of Python and R

```r
filter_by_reply_content_substring <- function(reply, substring_config, file_column_name) {
  # Get the list of substrings for the specific column name
  substrings <- substring_config[[file_column_name]]
  
  # If no substrings exist for this column, return unchanged data
  if (is.null(substrings) || length(substrings) == 0) {
    message(paste("No substrings found for column:", file_column_name))
    return(reply)
  }
  
  content_contains_re <- stri_c('(', stri_c(substrings, collapse = "|"), ')')
  
  # Find rows that do not match any of those substrings
  is_not_reply_with_substring <- !stri_detect_regex(reply[[file_column_name]], content_contains_re, case_insensitive = TRUE)
  
  # Return the filtered dataframe
  return(reply[is_not_reply_with_substring])
}
```

```r
filter_by_reply_content_substring <- function(reply, substring_conf, file_column_name) {
  # file_column_name can be one or more columns sent in as a vector
  for (col in file_column_name) {
    
    # Defensive check: make sure column exists
    if (!(col %in% colnames(reply))) {
      warning(paste("Column", col, "not found in reply dataframe — skipping."))
      next
    }

    # Get substrings for this column from config
    substrings <- substring_conf[[col]]
    
    # Skip if no substrings are defined for this column
    if (is.null(substrings) || length(substrings) == 0) {
      message(paste("No substrings found for column:", col, "— skipping."))
      next
    }

    content_contains_re <- stri_c('(', stri_c(substrings, collapse = "|"), ')')

    # Find rows that DO NOT match any of those substrings (case-insensitive)
    is_not_reply_with_substring <- !stri_detect_regex(reply[[col]], content_contains_re, case_insensitive = TRUE)

    # Apply the filter for this column
    reply <- reply[is_not_reply_with_substring, , drop = FALSE]

    message(paste("Applied substring filter for column:", col))
  }

  # Return the fully filtered dataframe
  return(reply)
}
```

```r
# Cleans comments from communication dataset
# Args:
#   df: A data frame containing 'if_comment', 'reply_subject', and 'reply_id' columns
# Returns:
#   A cleaned data frame with duplicates and irrelevant comments removed
clean_mbox_comment <- function(df) {
  if (!("if_comment" %in% colnames(df)) || !("reply_subject" %in% colnames(df)) || !("reply_id" %in% colnames(df))) {
    stop("The data frame does not contain required columns: 'if_comment', 'reply_subject', and 'reply_id'")
  }

  initial_row_count <- nrow(df)
  df <- df[!duplicated(df$reply_id), ]
  duplicate_rows_removed <- initial_row_count - nrow(df)

  subject_df <- df[df$if_comment == FALSE, ]
  comment_df <- df[df$if_comment == TRUE, ]

  initial_comment_row_count <- nrow(comment_df)
  valid_reply_ids <- subject_df$reply_id
  comment_df <- comment_df[comment_df$reply_subject %in% valid_reply_ids, ]

  comment_rows_removed <- initial_comment_row_count - nrow(comment_df)
  cleaned_df <- rbind(subject_df, comment_df)

  cat("Removed", duplicate_rows_removed, "duplicate rows\n")
  cat("Removed", comment_rows_removed, "irrelevant comment rows\n")
  return(cleaned_df)
}
```

After a lot and trial and error on #295 the following was learned:

 * GitHub Actions no longer accept files to be created on /tmp. Instead `$RUNNER_TEMP` should be used. See [this article](https://nesin.io/blog/temp-directory-path-github-actions). Changes were made accordingly.
 * Further, pip no longer can be used on global environment, which is required to install perceval. A venv must be created. Therefore, the github actions workflows were updated to reflect that. Also, Venv was placed above the directory all actions execute (which is `$RUNNER_TEMP`/kaiaulu/kaiaulu). Failing that, the Check will find the .venv folder within Kaiaulu, failing the pass.
 * Perceval restriction to use version 0.12.4 has been lifted, as I can now test on my local machine the more recent version. The workflows were updated to reflect the version that is being tested locally by me (as I do not have the bandwidth to test every possible version). 
 * OS X version on GitHub Actions was also updated.
 * Various actions versions were updated since they had since been deprecated. 

Perhaps the most substantial change was the addition to the `tmp` variable to `tools.yml`. This is because the way GitHub Actions determine the tmp folder is now different than a local machine (which is just `/tmp`). As such, Kaiaulu needs to know where to place the intermediate files when creating unit tests. In the long run, parameterizing this is beneficial because it accommodates Windows users. 

Something worth noting is the R/examples.R needs some work to diagnose why it keeps throwing warnings. I waste a substantial amount of time looking to solve them on Github Actions just to realize they were already there all along and were not the cause of the errors.

As I had to prototype this on an actual PR to see it is in working order, the changes will be bundled with #295 . This is not ideal, but the changes are isolated to tests, and .workflow folder, so it should be easy to tell them apart even in one commit.
